title: The passive: di-, tak-, kok-
goal: Master the most used and most often skipped part of Javanese grammar — a passive whose form depends on **who does the action**, and which Javanese uses far more often than the active.
bekal: forming the passive with *di-*, *tak-*, and *kok-* according to who does it
using the suffixes *-aké* (for someone else) and *-i* (applied to something)
recognizing *ke-*, which marks something that happened by accident

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Bagi tugas resik-resik
dialogs.intro: Guests are on their way, and Rini divides up the chores. A ngoko conversation almost entirely in the passive — exactly how real Javanese speakers talk when sharing out work.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Yan, kamaré tak sapu, terasé kokpel, ya?
lines.id: Yan, I'll sweep the room, and you mop the porch, OK?
lines.literal: Yan, room-the I sweep, porch-the you mop, yes?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: OK. What about the dirty plates?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Kuwi mengko dikumbah Ahmad. Dhèwèké wis janji.
lines.id: Ahmad will wash those later. He promised.
lines.literal: that later washed Ahmad. he already promise.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Klambi sing ana ing jemuran wis kokjupuk durung?
lines.id: Have you brought in the clothes from the line yet?
lines.literal: clothes which exist on drying-line already you-take not-yet?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Durung. Tulung jupukna, ya. Mengko taklempit dhéwé.
lines.id: Not yet. Get them for me, please. I'll fold them myself later.
lines.literal: not-yet. please take-for-me, yes. later I-fold myself.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Iya. Éh, gelasé mau kepidak, tugel.
lines.id: OK. Oh, the glass got stepped on earlier, it broke.
lines.literal: yes. oh, glass-the earlier stepped-on, broken.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Waduh. Ora apa-apa, mengko tak tukokké manèh.
lines.id: Oh dear. It's OK, I'll buy another one later.
lines.literal: oh-dear. not what-what, later I buy-for again.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Aja, tak ganti dhéwé waé. Salahku.
lines.id: No, I'll replace it myself. My fault.
lines.literal: don't, I replace myself just. fault-my.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Wis, ora usah dipikir. Ayo dirampungké dhisik.
lines.id: Never mind, don't worry about it. Come on, let's get it done first.
lines.literal: enough, no need thought. come-on finished first.

notes: **Notice how many passive sentences there are in this dialogue** — nearly all of them. In English these sentences would naturally be active ("I'll sweep the room"). In Javanese, **the passive is the standard form** when the doer is "I" or "you". The active sentence *aku nyapu kamaré* is correct, but sounds as if you are putting yourself forward.

**Kepidak** = *ke-* + *idak* (step on), "got stepped on". The prefix *ke-* marks something that happened by accident, like "get" in "got stepped on". You have already met the family: *kepeksa*, *kèri*, *kebablasen*, *kesasar*.
**Tugel** means "broken, snapped", used for hard things that break in two. For something shattered into pieces, use *pecah*.
**Tak tukokké** stacks two things: *tak-* (I, as the doer in a passive) and *-ké* (for someone else). It means "I'll buy (it) for you". Stacks like this are very common and will soon feel natural.
**Dirampungké** = *di-* + *rampung* + *-ké*, "be finished off". Notice that the suffix *-ké* turns the adjective *rampung* (finished) into an action done to something.
**Waduh** (oh no, oh dear) and **éh** (oh, hey) are exclamations. Javanese also has *lho*, *wah*, *hla*, *ta*, and *je*, which all color the sentence without changing its meaning.

grammars.title: Three passive prefixes, one for each doer
body: This is the part of Javanese with no counterpart in English. English uses one passive for everyone and adds the doer with "by" ("the book is read by me"). Javanese chooses **a different prefix** depending on who the doer is.
after: **In krama, all three merge into *dipun-*.** The doer is named separately if needed: *bukunipun dipunwaos kula* (the book, I read it). This is one place where krama is actually simpler than ngoko.
**Tak- and dak- mean the same**; *tak-* is more common in Yogyakarta and Solo, *dak-* elsewhere. The same goes for *kok-* and *ko-*.

**The active prefix N- you learned in unit 8 disappears** when the sentence becomes passive. *Nyapu* (active) → *taksapu* (passive, by me), not *taknyapu*. Go back to the root first, then attach the passive prefix.

grammars.title: Two suffixes that change the target
body: After the prefix come two suffixes that decide **what the action is done to**. You don't need to master them at once; it is enough to recognize the pieces.

head: Suffix
Meaning
Example
Translation
rows: for someone else, or cause to be

after: **-aké** points the action toward someone or makes something happen ("buy *for* you", "make finished"), while **-i** applies the action *to* a place or thing ("clean *the room*", "give *someone*"). English does the same job with prepositions and word order instead of suffixes.
These suffixes stack with the passive prefixes without trouble: *tak* + *tuku* + *ké* = **taktukokké** (I'll buy it for you); *di* + *resik* + *i* = **diresiki** (be cleaned).
At A1 you **don't need to build them fluently yourself**. What you need is to recognize the pieces when you hear them, so that a word as long as *dipunpriksakaken* doesn't feel like a wall.

blocks.text: This isn't just grammar; it is a way of seeing things. An active sentence puts **the doer** first: *aku nyapu kamar* — I am the one sweeping. A passive sentence puts **the task** first: *kamaré taksapu* — the room, which I'll sweep.

In a culture that avoids putting oneself forward, the second option feels more polite and more natural. That is why, in everyday conversation, **sentences with "I" or "you" as the doer are almost always passive**. You will sound far more Javanese if you get used to this pattern.

head: What a learner tends to say
What sounds more natural in Javanese

blocks.text: The sentences on the left are **not wrong** — they are all correct and understood. But you will hear the ones on the right far more often from Javanese speakers, and copying them is one of the small changes that most improves the impression you make.

blocks.title: A rule of thumb for A1
items: **When you talk about what you will do to a thing**, start with the thing, then attach *tak-* to the verb. *Piringé takumbah.*
**When you ask what the other person did to a thing**, start with the thing, then attach *kok-*. *Klambiné wis kokjupuk?*
**When the doer is someone else or unclear**, use *di-*. This is the closest to an ordinary passive, and the hardest to get wrong.

blocks.text: The prefix *ke-* marks something that happens to you without anyone intending it, like English "get" in "got lost" or "got left behind". It is very common, and some of its forms have even entered everyday Indonesian.

All these words can be used as they are, as verbs: *aku keturon* (I fell asleep), *HP-ku kegawa Rini* (Rini took my phone by mistake). Notice that the doer, if there is one, comes **after** the verb with no linking word.

exercises.prompt: Change these active sentences into the passive with the right prefix.
Write the *ke-* word for each situation.
**Review of Unit 16.** Cover Unit 16, then write these sentences in Javanese (ngoko).
items: When I was little I lived in a village.
Three years ago I moved to the city.
Yesterday I fell in the street.
It turned out my phone was in my bag.
